chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He was asked about the slaughtered animal that is slaughtered facing away from the Qibla, so he said, 'There is no harm if he did not intend it.' And about the man who slaughters and forgets to say the name of God, is his slaughtered animal eaten? He said, 'Yes, if he is not suspected [of negligence] and he was good at slaughtering before that, and he does not tear out the throat and does not break the neck until the animal cools down.'

key_terms.يَنْخَعُ: To tear out the throat (a specific method of slaughter)
key_terms.يُسَمِّيَ: To recite the name of God (Tasmiyah)

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a slaughtered animal's meat to be considered halal if the slaughterman forgets to say Bismillah or faces away from the Qibla?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that minor ritual deviations, such as facing away from the Qibla or forgetting the Tasmiyah, do not invalidate the slaughter provided there is no deliberate intent or professional incompetence. This ruling emphasizes the Shia principle of ease in dietary laws, requiring the slaughterman to be trustworthy (mu'tamad) and skilled in ensuring the animal is fully bled before death. The hadith underscores the importance of practical competence and integrity over rigid formalism in the permissibility of meat.
